item.title: Why do people respond differently to mosquito bites? A scientist explains
item.description: The reaction reflects a complex interaction between mosquito saliva and the immune system.
item.content:encoded:
Two people spend an evening in the same garden and receive roughly the same number of mosquito bites. By morning, one barely notices them – while the other is covered in large, swollen, intensely itchy welts that linger for days.

Most of us have experienced this, or know someone who has. But why is it that mosquito bites affect some people so differently? The answer lies in the way a mosquito’s saliva interacts with our unique immune system.

When a mosquito bites you, they inject saliva into your skin. The immune system recognises the saliva as foreign and releases histamine – an immune cell chemical that causes allergy symptoms such as redness, swelling and itchiness.

But this only partly explains what’s going on. A mosquito’s saliva also contains a range of other biologically active compounds that interact with the immune system in more complex ways than once assumed.

For instance, a mosquito’s saliva also contains proteins that prevent blood clotting and keep blood flowing so they can feed undisturbed.

These same salivary proteins influence the immune response that occurs at the bite site. Rather than acting solely as a feeding aid, mosquito saliva can alter the local immune environment within minutes of a bite.

item.title: ‘Worthy of derision’: HC on Noida official order to detain 25-year-old activist under NSA
item.description: The judges underlined that bureaucrats must ‘realise that their loyalty is towards the Constitution and not the political executive’.
item.content:encoded:
The Allahabad High Court has said that the Gautam Buddha Nagar district magistrate’s conduct in detaining a 25-year-old Delhi University graduate under the National Security Act after the workers’ protest in Noida “is worthy of derision”.

The Act allows for long periods of detention without trial up to a year.

Quashing the preventive detention of Akriti Chaudhary on Wednesday, the High Court said District Magistrate Medha Roopam was “guilty of violating her oath of allegiance”.

Chaudhary has been in jail for nearly five months. She was detained on April 11 during the workers’ protest in Noida. A month later, the National Security Act was invoked against her.

Despite her detention under the Act being quashed, she remains in jail because she has been named in several first information reports in connection with the protest.

The police had claimed that Chaudhary and 60-year-old Satya Verma, a journalist from Lucknow, were “significant in instigating violence, arson and creating chaos” during the protest. It also claimed that Verma and Chaudhary “provoked” persons in different areas to “disturb public order”.

item.title: Interview: Are data centres really ‘development’ for India?
item.description: Tech giants are getting land and resources with little guarantee of how local communities will benefit, says Osama Manzar of the Digital Empowerment Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
This article was originally published in Rest of World, which covers technology’s impact outside the West.

When Osama Manzar started the nonprofit Digital Empowerment Foundation in 2002, just 1.2% of India’s population was online. Now, more than 70% is. But Manzar’s mission statement – helping poor and rural communities come out of the digital dark to access information, literacy, and livelihoods – still holds.

In the age of artificial intelligence, Manzar senses the risk of another extractive technology, with the benefits and control concentrated among powerful actors both at the algorithmic level and in terms of land and water.

As protests erupt from India to Malaysia to Chile, Manzar – who has served on several Indian government and international policy committees dealing with internet access, digital inclusion, and infrastructure – not only questions how and where the data centers are being built, but also why. Especially when they’re on track to consume water equivalent to that of 1.3 billion people’s annual domestic needs, and require electricity matching the energy demand of 650 million people by 2030.

item.title: Monsoon Session not closed as Amit Shah ‘scrambling’ to pass delimitation bill, claims Congress
item.description: ‘Normally, prorogation takes place three to four days’ after a Parliament session is adjourned sine die, Jairam Ramesh pointed out.
item.content:encoded:
The Congress on Monday claimed that the Monsoon Session of Parliament had not been formally closed despite 25 days having passed since its adjournment because the Union government was “scrambling around” to find a majority for the delimitation bill.

The process of fixing the boundaries of electoral constituencies is called delimitation.

In a social media post, Congress leader Jairam Ramesh said that “normally, prorogation takes place three to four days” after a Parliament session is adjourned sine die.

However, the Union Home Minister Amit Shah had kept the Monsoon Session “on ventilator”, claimed Ramesh.

“How much longer before he accepts the reality that his politics of threats and intimidation has reached its limit?” asked the Rajya Sabha MP.

Today is exactly 25 days since Parliament was adjourned sine die. But it has still NOT been prorogued.

item.title: YouTuber Ajeet Bharti denied anticipatory bail for remarks about Bhim Army chief
item.description: There should be no apprehension of arrest only because a case had been registered, held the bench.

A Delhi court on Monday rejected YouTuber Ajeet Bharti’s petition seeking anticipatory bail in a case pertaining to his allegedly derogatory and casteist remarks about Azad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram) MP Chandra Shekhar Aazad, Bar and Bench reported.

Aazad is the president of the party and the chief of the Dalit rights organisation Bhim Army.

The first information report against Bharti was filed based on a complaint by the Azad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram) on August 23.

The party alleged Bharti made “caste-based, abusive, humiliating, sexually degrading and potentially inflammatory statements” about the Nagina MP and about BR Ambedkar in a video where he spoke about the anti-reservation protests held at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar in August.

On Monday, Additional Sessions Judge Saurabh Pratap Singh Laler held that Bharti’s plea for anticipatory bail was not maintainable, reported Bar and Bench.

item.title: Fiction: Radhika’s husband sets bizarre rules for her. Then something happens at her child’s school
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Moms’, by Shivani Sibal.
item.content:encoded:
Manik Khanna had a list; he was a methodical man. Crime and punishment were clearly spelt out, leaving little room for uncertainty, doubt or confusion. What had begun as a game between husband and wife proved so effective that it endured long past its lascivious origins. He had handwritten the rules and locked the pages away in his safe, nothing digital. Aside from the infringements listed in the agreement, Radhika was free to do as she pleased. It seemed fair to him.

He spent years contemplating what to include in the list, carefully observing Radhika in the early days of their marriage as he compiled it – her personality, her flaws, what he could tolerate and what he couldn’t, what she could endure and what she couldn’t. Sherawat alleged that Chaudhary had described him as an “anti-national”.

“It was a mala fide act, meant to discredit a critic of the government, to paint a peaceful protest as anti-national, and to expose the plaintiff to public hatred and to danger,” read his petition.

Sherawat has sought Rs 5 crore in damages from Chaudhary, his production company Essprit Productions and Doordarshan News.

The 28-year-old had been part of the protests against alleged mismanagement of several competitive examinations, which began on June 6. item.title: Dhirendra Shastri’s call for Hindus to avoid ‘dirty’ non-veg during Durga Puja sparks TMC criticism
item.description: After the religious leader said that meat must not be sold near the goddess’ idol, the TMC asserted that Bengalis will ‘not let this go’.
item.content:encoded:
Dhirendra Shastri, the head of the Bageshwar Dham temple, on Sunday said that Hindus must avoid eating non-vegetarian food during the Durga Puja festival and at pandals in West Bengal. The Trinamool Congress said that Bengalis “will not let go” if somebody tries to dictate what they eat or celebrate their festival.

Speaking at an event in Kolkata, Shastri said he does not like it when “dirty” non-vegetarian food is eaten during Durga Puja and at gatherings linked to the festivities.

“I want the Hindus of Kolkata to awaken and boycott such people,” he said. “…[These people] cannot be considered religious.”

Meat must not be sold near the goddess’ idol during the festival, he added.

The festival will begin on October 6 and conclude on October 10 this year.

Eating meat during Durga Puja is common among Bengali Hindus and animal sacrifice is an important ritual for some in the community.

item.title: A new book on Indian laws demystifies the ‘right to privacy’ and examines how it has improved lives
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Trials of a Nation: How Crises, Conflicts and Courts Shaped Modern India’, by Priya Jain.
item.content:encoded:
Justice Jasti Chelameswar focused on the distinction between “freedom from intrusion” and “freedom of decision”. He emphasised that a fundamental right need not be expressly stated in the Constitution to exist.

Justice SA Bobde articulated that privacy is the “condition precedent” for the exercise of other rights. Without privacy, can one truly exercise freedom of speech or religion? He argued that privacy belongs to the individual, not the state. Justice Manohar Sapre based the right to privacy on the Preamble’s values of liberty and dignity, stating that these values cannot exist without privacy.

Justice RF Nariman, in a scholarly opinion, followed the history of fundamental rights and explicitly overruled the infamous ADM Jabalpur judgment, correcting a 40-year-old historical wrong.

Justice SK Kaul focused on the age of digital technology, referring to the term “digital footprints”. He recognised the concept of the “right to be forgotten” and warned against the dangers of profiling and big data.

The nine judges unanimously declared: “The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.”

This judgment unequivocally settled the specific legal question and further redefined the framework of fundamental...

item.title: Singapore must never allow prejudice against any community: PM Lawrence Wong on anti-Indian abuse
item.description: The police were investigating racist posts about the Nepal-China flash flood and Singapore Airlines’ investment in Air India, the Wong government said.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore must never allow prejudice against any community to become normalised, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on Sunday about online abuse targeting persons of Indian origin in the country.

The comments came a day after Singaporean Home Minister K Shanmugam said that the police were investigating “nasty and racist” posts online about the Nepal-China flash flood and Singapore Airlines’ investment in Air India.

Shanmugam said that the comments had been directed at Singaporeans of Indian ethnicity, including the chief executive officer of the state-owned investment firm Temasek, and Indians in general.

On Sunday, Wong said that “an uglier side” had emerged in online discussions about the two matters.

The allegedly racist comments on social media were relating to some of the Singaporeans missing in the disaster in Nepal, Wong said. Some posts questioning the Singaporean national airline’s 25% stake in Air India had been “accompanied by anti-Indian abuse”, he said.

“We can and should have robust debates,” Wong said on social media. “But we should never use seemingly legitimate arguments as a cover to fuel prejudice against any community or hostility towards foreigners.”

The first information report has been registered against the attacker, who was arrested on Friday.

item.title: Maharashtra: VHP calls for barring Muslims from garba events, demands Aadhaar checks
item.description: The Vishva Hindu Parishad said that organisers must apply a tilak on the foreheads of those participating in the Hindu festival.
item.content:encoded:
The Vishva Hindu Parishad has called for a ban on Muslims from taking part in garba events in Maharashtra and set “guidelines” for the organisers to verify the identity of participants, India Today reported on Sunday.

The measures include checking the Aadhaar cards of those participating and applying a tilak, a sacred mark on the forehead in Hindu tradition, on the participants.

VHP spokesperson Shriraj Nair said that the Hindutva group had decided to prevent Muslims from participating in garba events, arguing that the festival is centred on worshipping a Hindu deity, India Today reported.

Garba is a Gujarati folk dance, performed in a circular pattern around a lamp or idol, symbolising the Hindu deity Durga. It is performed during the festival of Navratri, which will begin on October 11 and end on October 20 this year.

“Navratri is not just about songs and dance,” Nair was quoted as saying. “The festival is about worshipping the goddess. Why should Muslims, who are against idol worship, participate in the festival?”

Hindutva groups have long tried to make the identity verification of those participating in garba and dandiya events mandatory to prevent “love jihad”.

item.title: As RSS chief Bhagwat’s UK plans are kept under wraps, protestors symbolically gather near Parliament
item.description: Demonstrators said they were questioning the silence of British officials on the Hindutva organisation’s majoritarian ideology.
item.content:encoded:
When Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat arrived in Britain on September 3 on the last leg of an international tour that had started in the US on August 25 and also taken him to Canada, no exact schedule had been made public.

Despite not having any confirmation of his movements, protesters gathered outside Parliament Square in London on Sunday, the day before Bhagwat’s visit was expected to conclude.

With the Houses of Parliament and Big Ben serving as a symbolic backdrop, the demonstrators aimed to send two messages: that they rejected the Hindu majoritarianism of the RSS and were rebuking the UK for its official silence on the visit.

Participants from an array of campaign organisations, diaspora groups, students and academics assembled through the afternoon, Palestine flags mixed in with placards reading, “Never Forget Gujarat Genocide, 2002”, “Diaspora united against fascism” and “Inquilab Zindabad” – long live the revolution. Another sign addressed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham: “Will you ban RSS?”

item.title: Start the week with a film: In ‘Unidentified’, lifting the veil off murder in a conservative society
item.description: Haifaa al-Mansour’s Arabic film is out on Prime Video.
item.content:encoded:
Cultural context is everything in Unidentified (2025). The film’s synopsis – a woman who is a fan of true crime shows gets obsessed with identifying a murdered Jane Doe – sounds garden variety. But the setting – Riyadh in conservative Saudi Arabia – makes all the difference.

Nawal (Mila Alzahrani) works at a police station’s archive, digitising files all day long. She’s the only woman around when her boss Majid (Shafi Al Harthi) is informed about a dead teenager lying in the desert. The girl, later named as Amal, is going to be buried in an unmarked grave.

Although it’s none of Nawal’s business, she makes it her own. Over Majid’s objections, Nawal starts investigating Amal’s background. Nawal runs into barriers every step of the way – at Amal’s school, from her circle of friends, and finally from her family.

Notions of honour, propriety and shame hang over the case. It appears that nobody in Amal’s orbit wants her to be identified, let alone explain what she was doing at the murder site meeting a man. item.title: Remembering ‘Got Japan’: This book dissects upper-caste life in Himalayan towns in colonised India
item.description: An excerpt from the Introduction to ‘Brahmins of the Himalaya: Upper-Caste Ways of Belonging, 1850-1950’, by Sanjay Joshi.
item.content:encoded:
In 1906, a young Brahmin named Bholadutt Pande decided to travel to Japan and the United States to seek better educational opportunities than were available to him in British India. He was the first from his community of elite Almora Brahmins to make a journey crossing the seas, at least in recent memory. His return to Almora in 1910 sparked a huge controversy. Overseas travel was regarded as taboo for caste-Hindus. It was impossible, some Hindus argued, to sustain the required levels of ritual purity – an essential component of caste – through a long sea voyage and an extended sojourn abroad. So Bholadutt’s return polarised the community.

Several families in Almora bore the brunt of the controversy created by Pande’s travel overseas. With such virulence did the debate on his return escalate that it created a huge schism among clans. The divisions were pretty serious – inter-family and even intra-family. Daughters could not meet mothers on account of their opposing views of the affair, fathers refused to eat with their sons, uncles ostracised nephews, brothers refused to talk to brothers – all on account of a difference of opinion on what Bholadutt Pande’s status should be. item.title: In a first, Gauhati HC asks Assam government to pay Rs 2 lakh to woman pushed into Bangladesh
item.description: Mumtaz Begum had been arrested from Nagaon foreigners tribunal in violation of the court order.
item.content:encoded:
The Gauhati High Court has directed the Assam government to pay Rs 2 lakh as compensation to a Bengali-origin Muslim woman for expelling her to Bangladesh.

This is the first time any court has imposed a cost on the state for forcing out a person to Bangladesh, in violation of deportation rules.

As Scroll had reported, Mumtaz Begum’s family realised she had been forced out of the country when they filed a habeas corpus petition in the Gauhati High Court.

The High Court impleaded the Ministry of External Affairs in the case and said it would direct it to “make an endeavour to have the woman located in Bangladesh and to expatriate her to India”.

The court also came down heavily on the Nagaon foreigners tribunal for its role in Begum’s expulsion.

Acting on the habeas corpus petition, the bench of Justice Kalyan Rai Surana and Justice Susmita Phukan Khaund said the court is satisfied from the nature of action taken by the foreigners tribunal that “the element of malice in law on part of the learned tribunal is apparent on the face of record.”

Foreigners tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies unique to Assam that decide on matters of nationality on the basis of documentary evidence.

item.title: Long gaps between meals affect older people differently, shows study
item.description: Ageing changes how people digest food, absorb nutrients, control blood sugar and maintain muscle.
item.content:encoded:
Going for much of the day without eating is often promoted as a way to improve health or lose weight. But a new study suggests that long gaps between meals may have different effects on older adults – especially those in the oldest age groups.

For the study, my colleagues and I followed nearly 3,000 people aged 60 and over in Sweden and found that those who usually went longest without eating developed chronic diseases faster than those who had shorter gaps between meals. The difference was clearest among people aged 78 and over.

This does not mean that fasting causes disease in old age, nor that every older person should avoid long intervals without food. But it does raise questions about whether advice based on studies of younger and middle-aged adults can be safely applied to older age groups.

Fasting helps the body switch from using readily available sugar to using stored energy, such as fat. Studies in younger adults have linked some forms of fasting to better control of blood sugar and other potentially beneficial changes in metabolism. A recent review found that intermittent fasting led to modest weight loss and some improvements in metabolic health compared with eating without restrictions.

item.title: ‘Kin’: Tayari Jones’s new novel is a story of and by women, and of their shared passions
item.description: The force of the Civil Rights Movement shapes the horizon of the characters as they navigate jobs, friendships, romances, grief, and dreams.
item.content:encoded:
I found myself reading slowly through Tayari Jones’s new novel, Kin till the second half, where it opened up like a flower that had been tightly furled for too long. By the final pages, I realised the significance of its epigraph – “We are each other’s business.”

At its heart, Kin is a story of and by women.

The men in the novel play their roles well. They hurt, comfort, disappoint, leave, and stay. But it is the women who are its heart. Every time I thought I understood them, they revealed yet another hidden history, an old grief, a private resilience.

The remarkable women

Hattie Lee is perhaps the best example of this. Initially dismissed as “trifling”, she slowly emerges as a woman shaped by suffering, endurance, and survival. Another character, Babydoll, enters the story as the “other woman” for Annie, someone she is primed to resent. She calls herself and Annie a “package deal” to get them both employed in the new city. When their boss’s wife arrives to accuse her of sleeping with her husband, Babydoll stands as a defiant comrade instead of revealing the truth of what was actually Annie’s affair. It is an unusual relationship indeed and perhaps, only Jones could have written it.

item.title: In a surprising reversal of trends, world’s mangrove forests are expanding
item.description: What’s driving this? And could it help curb climate change?
item.content:encoded:
Mangroves are perplexing plants.

They breathe through their roots, appear to stand on stilts and grow best in hot, salty seawater drawn in and out by the tide.

Historically, mangrove forests have been dismissed as inhospitable places to avoid and have been extensively cleared. But these fascinating trees are now gaining attention for how they support biodiversity, store carbon and buffer the effects of storms, cyclones and tsunamis.

Since 1984, scientists have been monitoring the growth and geographical reach of mangrove forests using satellites. And for the first time, these unique ecosystems are expanding at a faster rate than they are declining.

So what’s driving this? And could it help curb climate change?

Why mangroves matter

Mangrove forests were long viewed as largely expendable places. Research shows people were quick to convert them into rice paddies, oil palm plantations and aquaculture operations. Some were even used as rubbish tips.

However, mangrove forests are now recognised as a vital part of our coastal environments. They provide habitat for a wealth of plants and animals including fish such as barramundi and giant shovelnose rays, reptiles such as seasnakes and even mammals such as the proboscis monkey and water mouse. They are crucial carbon stores, locking up roughly four times more carbon than other land-based forests. Mangroves can also shelter coastal communities and ecosystems from natural disasters by reducing the risk of flooding and erosion.

item.description: Jing-Jing Lee’s 2019 novel is inspired by the stories of her own family.

“I arrived home, or where it used to be, and all that was left was a wreckage. Just ash and charred wood where our lives used to be. There was a big patch in front of the houses where the earth had been turned over and patted down. I lowered myself into a squat, put my hand to the ground. There was nothing left. It was as if I had dreamed it all, what happened. I was the only one who could prove it but the only evidence I had was the absence of things…”

Few nations in the world have tried to redeem their colonial past as assiduously as Japan. The kawaii-fication of Japan, an aesthetisation of “cuteness”, emerged from the devastation of the Second World War. It gained serious momentum in the 1980s and ’90s when Japanese anime culture, along with kawaii, began earning fans across the globe. Today, Japan is revered for its strong cultural identity, delicious food, and enviable professional efficiency. It is a top tourist destination and immigrants have found ways to assimilate, despite language and cultural barriers.

item.title: ‘The Grave Exhumers and Other Stories’: A close-up of Muslim lives outside Kolkata’s urban premises
item.description: The six stories by Lutfor Rahaman have been translated from the Bengali by Mursed Alam.
item.content:encoded:
The stories in The Grave Exhumers and Other Stories by Lutfor Rahaman were written when he was 21 years old. To be 21 and have such a deep-rooted grasp of the colour, habitation, geography, and taste of the air is remarkable to witness. And what’s more impressive is the fact that translator Mursed Alam has managed to get these details and idiosyncrasies without diluting them.

Comprising six short stories, the collection zeroes down on death in some or the other form. For instance, even a seemingly optimistic story (at least by the title) called “Collectors of Hope”, starts thus: “Sohrab lost the job, finally!”

A world on the margins

Death looms over the reader like a crow perched on an ever-drying branch. Through death, Rahaman manages to construct a world on the margins, all set in a village on the outskirts of Kolkata. The stories become important because they provide a foil to the canonical Bengali literature – the Tagores and the Chattopadhyays – and take us down to the cellular level of the lives of Muslim communities in rural areas.

item.title: Chhattisgarh: NIA court convicts 10 persons in 2013 Jhiram Valley Maoist attack
item.description: Congress’ state unit chief Nand Kumar Patel and party leader Mahendra Karma, who was key in organising the Salwa Judum, had been killed in the ambush.
item.content:encoded:
A National Investigation Agency court on Saturday convicted 10 persons accused in the 2013 Jhiram Valley Maoist attack that killed 29 persons, including senior Congress leaders, reported The Indian Express.

NIA judge Ajay Singh Rajput will announce the sentence on September 16.

On May 25, 2013, more than 150 Maoists had ambushed a Congress convoy in Bastar’s Jhiram Ghati ahead of Assembly elections. Among those killed were Congress’ state unit chief Nand Kumar Patel and his son Dinesh, and former MLA Uday Mudliyar.

Party leader Mahendra Karma, who played an instrumental role in organising the anti-Maoist state-sponsored militia Salwa Judum, was also killed in the attack.

The campaign was launched in 2005 to target villages seen as harbouring Maoists. Armed vigilantes allegedly torched homes and forced villagers to flee to government-run camps.

Translated as “purification hunt” in the Gondi language, Salwa Judum was presented by the state government as a spontaneous movement by the region’s Adivasi community against the Maoists.

However, human rights activists have accused the Salwa Judum of coercing residents into leaving their villages and supporting the group. With the tribal community split between both sides, there were several deaths over several months.

An investigation into the Jhiram Valley attack showed that it was primarily targeted at Karma, reported The Indian Express.

item.title: Dolly Parton and Gloria Steinem: Two ways to fight for women’s freedoms
item.description: ‘Feminism means each of us finding our unique power, and helping other women do the same,’ Steinem wrote about Parton.
item.content:encoded:
Two legends passed away in this past month – Dolly Parton and Gloria Steinem. While each has a distinct and vastly different persona, I see them both as pioneers of women’s rights and freedoms. Each did a great deal in entirely different ways to advance women’s rights and both were known far beyond America.

Dolly was not driven by a scripted feminist ideology nor did she preach it – she lived the life of a liberated woman defying stereotypes of what women should look, sound like, be and do.

Gloria, founder of Ms magazine and often considered a leader of the Second Wave Feminist movement was a fierce advocate of women’s rights and reproductive freedoms and spear-headed women’s protest movements for more than 50 years.

Dolly Parton is hardly anybody’s idea of a feminist icon but she certainly was one for me. Her over-the-top wigs, heavy rhinestone studded sexy costumes, huge bust, pinched waist and numerous plastic surgeries that she joked about to look the way she wanted to look could distract many from her surefootedness as a very astute businesswoman who made it in a man’s world.

item.title: Ramachandra Guha: For 120 years, Indian students have fought to change politics and public life
item.description: A short history of student movements, from the swadeshi agitation in Bengal to the Cockroach Janta Party-led protests.

In early July, as the students’ protests in Jantar Mantar were taking shape, the Trinamool Congress MP, Mahua Moitra, was one of the first politicians to show up in person and offer solidarity. Three weeks later, when the Union education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, resigned, Moitra thanked the younger generation “for saving Indian democracy” by bringing “this fascist, arrogant government to its knees”.

This, as she pointed out, was something the Opposition parties had not been able to do in the past 12 years.

Mahua Moitra’s praise was well merited. item.title: Consumers can’t get enough pistachio – but concerns about its environmental impact are growing
item.description: The crop has a large carbon footprint and is worryingly water-intensive.
item.content:encoded:
Pistachio production has more than trebled in the last 20 years. In 2024, more than 1.4 million tonnes were produced globally. Their popularity has only increased in the last two years, with a growing status as a trendy, luxury food item.

However, this rise in popularity has come with concerns around the pistachio’s environmental impacts. There are also questions around whether their production can withstand changing climate conditions.

Pistachios originated in modern-day Turkey and Iran. Despite being considered a nut, they are actually the seeds of pistachio trees. These trees thrive in a hot summer climate but require relatively cold winter temperatures to ensure the trees flower at the right time in spring. They also require dry conditions, as high humidity can reduce yields and leave the trees susceptible to fungal disease.

In the late 19th and early 20th century, pistachios were popularised in the US by migrants from the Middle East. By the 1930s, pistachio orchards were established in California. The warm, dry climate of California provided ideal conditions for pistachio trees, so much so that the US has now overtaken Iran and Turkey as the world’s largest producer of pistachios.

item.title: ‘The Anniversary’: This Italian novel examines a patriarchal nuclear family and its links to fascism
item.description: A post-traumatic memoir of survival in which the narrator calmly recalls the turbulence of the past.
item.content:encoded:
Andrea Bajani’s novel, the winner of the 2025 Strega Prize, is a radical exploration of the psychology of family estrangement. It appears at a cultural moment where therapy-oriented language such as “gaslighting”, “boundaries”, and “toxic” has percolated into the most intimate realms of daily life and adult children are fearlessly breaking taboos and going no-contact with their parents by denouncing the abuse within highly dysfunctional households. The Anniversary examines the social institution of the patriarchal nuclear family and its links to fascism in Italy, showing how domestic violence and coercive control by male members of the family are rendered invisible and normative.

The totalitarian infrastructures

In the novel, following a series of “unreliable memories”, the narrator recalls events that led to the final goodbye with his parents ten years ago. With the dysfunctional family at its centre, The Anniversary is an intensely psychological novel. Yet it does not treat the trauma of upbringing as a problem that can be solved through psychoanalysis. Instead, it moves outward to reflect on wider social conditions that allow totalitarian values to be reproduced in the private realms of the modern nuclear family.

The Pitt Rivers Museum, which holds collections from Oxford University, has the world’s largest Naga collection. It has around 8,000 Naga objects, including human remains, mainly skulls, and 178 objects that contain or may contain human hair. Skulls and other body parts were often taken from Asia, Africa and elsewhere to Britain and other former colonial powers as “trophies”, and were traded, displayed or studied.

The remaining 31 deaths were on the Chinese side of the border, Chinese news agency Xinhua reported.

Nearly 5,000 persons, including 618 foreigners, were missing in Nepal and more than 500 in China. Those missing in Nepal included 275 Indians, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Friday.

It Started with Words: The Epidemic of Hate Speech in New India, Harsh Mander

Since 2014, hate speech in India has moved from the political fringe to the centre of public life. It is heard from election platforms and religious stages, repeated in television studios, circulated through WhatsApp and YouTube, and rewarded with votes, influence and profit. It calls for minorities to be boycotted, evicted, stripped of their livelihoods, driven from neighbourhoods and, increasingly, met with violence.

These words have consequences. They create the climate in which homes and shops are demolished, and ordinary citizens are lynched, intimidated, and made to prove, again and again, that they belong to their own country.

Human rights activist Harsh Mander examines how this hatred is produced, spread and protected; who profits from it; and what happens when those who incite fear also command the machinery of the state. Drawing on several case studies, including his own attempt to seek legal action against politicians for incendiary speeches delivered in the lead-up to the communal riots in Delhi in 2020, Mander asks whether the law can still protect the vulnerable – or whether it has become another weapon in the hands of the powerful.

item.title: United Nations adopts new map showing Africa larger
item.description: The United States was the only country to oppose the resolution to replace the 16th century Mercator projection that enlarged landmasses closer to the poles.
item.content:encoded:
The United Nations General Assembly on Friday adopted a new world map that makes the African continent appear larger and shrinks North America and Europe.

The nonbinding resolution piloted by Togo was aimed at adopting a more accurate representation of continental landmasses. While it was supported by 164 countries, including India, six countries abstained from voting. The United States was the only country to vote against the resolution.

The new map, known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection, improves the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the continents. Created by a group of cartographers in 2018, the new map makes Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania appear much larger.

It replaces the 16th century Mercator projection, still the most widely used map in the world. It was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to solve a maritime navigation problem. Because straight lines on his map correspond to constant compass directions, sailors could use it to plot their courses, the United Nations noted.

However, while preserving directions, landmasses closer to the poles appear increasingly enlarged than those near the equator. For example, Greenland looks roughly the same size as Africa, even though the latter is about 14 times larger.

item.title: In Odisha, drum-making traditions echo the rhythms of farm life

In Pahandi, a small village in Bijepur block of Odisha’s Bargarh district, the rhythm of a traditional baja or drum begins long before it reaches a festival ground. It begins with the earth.

Of the roughly 530 households in the village, most depend on agriculture, growing paddy, millets, green gram, ground nuts and other crops. But for eight households of the Chamar community, making traditional drums and other percussion instruments has supplemented their livelihoods for generations.

For Judhisthir Sagar, locally known as “Kutru”, the two occupations have always existed alongside each other. He inherited the craft of making baja from his ancestors, along with the practice of farming.

“Making drums and musical instruments is our identity,” said Sagar while tightening the strips of a newly made mrudanga, a two-headed percussion instrument widely used in traditional music. “We have been doing it for generations. It is our livelihood. We are proud to continue it.”

Apart from the mrudanga, other percussion instruments made in Pahandi include the godi mrudanga, udand khol, madol khol, dubi-tabla, pankuch, dhol and nisan. Each has a different shape and sound and a place in the cultural life of western Odisha.

item.title: Harsh Mander: Hindutva’s boycott calls seek the economic erasure of India’s Muslims
item.description: Through the Narendra Modi years, hateful calls have been amplified shrilly by affiliates of the Sangh, wrapped often in dangerous, even genocidal hate speech.
item.content:encoded:
The organised economic boycott of vulnerable and oppressed communities has scarred Indian society for millennia. India’s caste system excluded “untouchable” castes from employment in dignified vocations for since ancient times. This cruel arrangement has trapped them for centuries in want and penury, in illiteracy and in humiliating vocations.

The core of the Sangh project is to thrust Muslims into this same depressed zone.

Boycotts in history have also been a force for good. The boycott of foreign goods in colonial India led by Mahatma Gandhi shook the British Empire. When Rosa Parks in the United States in 1955 was found guilty of violating the Jim Crow racial segregation laws by refusing to vacate her seat in a bus for a white passenger, the Black community boycotted the bus system for 381 days. This brought the bus companies close to ruin, and the US Supreme Court judged the segregation laws to be unconstitutional.

However, the boycotts organised by the Sangh are part of their ambitious malevolent project of Hindu supremacism and anti-Muslim hate. Kenyan President William Ruto on Thursday said that he has ordered India’s Tata Chemicals to stop operations in the country, saying that its presence had failed to benefit his country, the BBC reported.

It has sought time till February to complete the exercise.

Though India’s struggle for independence was largely non-violent, it was constantly shadowed and vitalised by a relatively small but vocal and, at times, highly effective terrorist movement. The movement began in the 1870s as a reaction against the way in which the colonial government set about responding to the political trauma of 1857.

As we saw elsewhere, most Indians thought that the government in London was sympathetic to their aspirations, but that its good intentions were systematically frustrated by its narrow-minded representatives in India. Where is the Wi-Fi, the youngest, Joe (Phoenix Laroche), keeps plaintively asking. When handed a copy of Louisa May Alcott’s Little Women, the eldest, Beth (Delilah Bennett-Cardy), scoffs: this is about the oppression of the patriarchy. Also Beth: trees are literally the more boring things in the world.

item.title: For months, Adivasi children in Madhya Pradesh kept dying. The government woke up too late
item.description: Scroll travelled to Balaghat to investigate the mysterious outbreak. We found an absent state and lack of healthcare facilities had led to at least 25 deaths.
item.content:encoded:
Mahasingh Parte lives in the last hut in a village on the border of Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.

To reach the village, Matla, one has to trek a kilometre up a hill, on muddy trails and slippery slopes.

The village in Balaghat district in eastern Madhya Pradesh is surrounded by rolling hills and forests, a picture of tranquility for tourists visiting the nearby Kanha National Park.

But for Parte and other members of the Baiga tribe, who live in this remote region, life is a daily struggle – with little help forthcoming from the government.

Parte earns a living by collecting and selling tendu leaves and forest produce or labouring on other farms. The hut itself is bare except for a few steel utensils stacked in one dark corner. He grows millet and forages for seeds, other than depending on government ration.

“If we can manage, we eat two meals a day,” he told Scroll. “On many days, my children eat just once.”

In May, Parte’s four-year-old son Samlu caught a high fever. Soon, his six-year-old daughter Shamku’s body also felt warm.

One by one, all his five children fell ill.

item.title: How the US war has changed power equations in Iran
item.description: The fight is no longer about whether to bargain but the precise ways and means of improving Iran’s position before it commits to anything irreversible.
item.content:encoded:
When Washington unveiled its economic “D-Day” on August 19, the latest tightening of the financial siege and the blockade around Iran’s ports, it believed it was applying decisive leverage. But in Tehran the move was read as something else entirely – as confirmation that the US still prefers pressure to any settlement it might one day have to honour.

Across a political system that agrees on almost nothing, the interpretation was remarkably uniform. The economic stabilisers around the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, saw the US as reneging on a deal, while Ahmad Vahidi’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commanders saw their own warnings about American perfidy vindicated.

So whatever faith remained in Iran about US willingness to close a deal has thinned further. That erosion of trust now shapes what Tehran will and will not accept.

It is important to realise that Iran is making existential decisions about the survival strategy of the Islamic Republic itself. The old vocabulary of reformist against principlist – or moderate against hardliner – no longer reflects the real struggle inside the system.

Pecchi could not have guessed that the parangi who was leading her to this strange place was Schwartz – a man whose footsteps would later leave wide imprints on the soil of Thanjavur, whose name would one day be whispered as the shepherd of a new faith. For nearly 40 years, since Bartholomaeus Ziegenbalg had planted the first fragile seed of the Lutheran Mission in Tranquebar, Christianity had tried to push its tender roots into the hard earth of the south. item.title: Why Bangladesh should not join the Mecca Pact just to appease Pakistan or send a signal to India
item.description: The three members have pursued their own national interests, often at each other’s expense. Dhaka has no reason to behave differently.

When Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman told parliament last week that Dhaka would view an invitation to join the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement positively, he framed the country's possible participation as “a measure for the self-defense of the global Muslim community”.

“It is an internal matter of the Muslim family,” Rahman explained.

In India, where the prospect of Bangladesh joining a defence pact founded by Pakistan has drawn considerable attention, that framing has understandably fed suspicion.

For readers on each side of the border, it would be worth trying to understand why the pact's existing members would want Bangladesh in the first place and what Dhaka stands to gain – or lose – by joining in.

The Mecca Pact, signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan on August 7, remains a loosely defined arrangement.

Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has called it “purely defensive”, while Türkiye’s Hakan Fidan has likened its core clause to NATO's Article 5, which commits members to mutual defence.

Mechanisms for coordinating senior officials and armed forces are still being developed, and the pact lacks anything resembling NATO's integrated command structure.

item.title: Gloria Steinem, writer and feminist activist, dies at 92
item.description: One of the most prominent voices for reproductive rights, she spent two years in India in the 1950s and said the experience had a ‘huge influence on her’.
item.content:encoded:
Gloria Steinem, American writer and one of the most prominent activists for the reproductive and civil rights of women in the United States, died on Wednesday. She was 92.

She died at her home in New York, her foundation said on social media. “Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” it added.

Steinem started as a journalist in the 1960s, writing a feature on contraception that detailed how women were forced to choose between motherhood and careers. She followed this with an expose on sexism faced by cocktail waitresses at nightclubs owned and operated by Playboy Enterprises.

In 1971, she founded the Ms. magazine, a feminist publication that focused on problems faced by women.

She had moved from writing to public speaking after 1969, when she attended a meeting where women spoke up about the experience of having abortions, reported AFP.

Steinen had founded the National Women’s Political Caucus in 1971 with former US Representatives Bella Abzug and ​Shirley Chisholm and writer Betty Friedan.

item.title: Gloria Steinem (1934–2026): What we learnt from her 2015 memoir, ‘My Life on the Road’
item.description: One of the globally acknowledged leaders of second-wave feminism, Gloria Steinem died in her New York City home on September 2, 2026 at the age of 92.
item.content:encoded:
This article was originally published on The Conversation in 2018.

Gloria Steinem’s first book in more than a decade hit bookstores a couple of weeks ago. My Life on the Road proffers autobiographical snippets from what the famed feminist activist, journalist and author claims is the “most important, longest-running, yet least visible part of my life” – her nomadic existence on the road.

Steinem maintains that her intentions in relaying these experiences are manifold. Clearly, she wants to acquaint the public with this lesser-known facet of her itinerant life, but she also declares that she wants to “encourage you to spend some time on the road, too”; for us all “to share stories”; and “to open up the road – literally” given that “so far its been overwhelmingly masculine turf”.

item.title: Bar councils do not have power to punish law students, rules Supreme Court
item.description: The directions issued by the BCI chairperson to defer the enrolment of NALSAR’s graduating batch as advocates were unlawful, the court held.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Thursday held that the Bar Council of India and state bar councils do not have the statutory power to take disciplinary or punitive action against law students, Live Law reported.

The bar councils get disciplinary powers over law students only after they enrol as advocates, the court said.

It also held that the directions issued by Bar Council of India chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra on August 13 with respect to the graduating batch of students at the National Academy of Legal Studies and Research were unlawful, Live Law reported.

Mishra had directed state bar councils to defer the enrolment of the graduating batch as advocates after the students campaigned against inviting Chief Justice Surya Kant to their convocation over his remarks on police action against youth protesters. The Bar Council of India’s order had also sought an inquiry against the students and faculty members. The council, however, withdrew the directive hours later.

A day after the directive was issued, the Supreme Court had passed an interim order protecting NALSAR students and faculty members from punitive action by the Bar Council of India or any state bar council. Kant had described the bar council’s order as “absolutely uncalled for”.

The final details of India’s trade deal with the United States will be announced once Washington is able to give New Delhi a tariff advantage over competing countries, Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Thursday.

At an event in New Delhi, Goyal claimed that India had secured a good deal in “every sensitive sector”, such as agriculture, fisheries and micro, small and medium enterprises.

He added that the country’s goods exports had continued to grow in August and urged industry associations to set ambitious export targets.

Goyal also pointed to India’s 7.8% gross domestic product growth in the April-June quarter, saying it was “no mean achievement” against the backdrop of global uncertainty. He urged stakeholders not to be swayed by “naysayers”.

The Congress had questioned the GDP numbers on Tuesday, describing them as “statistical gymnastics” being used to hide “India’s bleak economic reality”.

The Supreme Court on Thursday refused to entertain a public interest litigation challenging orders by the Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan governments restricting the entry into public schools of outsiders, journalists, YouTubers and civil society representatives, Live Law reported.

The Bharatiya Janata Party government in both states had also mandated that permission must be taken for photography, videography, interviews, audio recording and livestreaming inside schools.

The orders had come against the backdrop of a nationwide drive of the Cockroach Janta Party political campaign to improve the condition of government schools. The campaign has been sharing videos of schools on social media recorded by its volunteers in several states.

The Rajasthan government had issued the order on August 16. In Uttar Pradesh, the basic education officer in Ayodhya issued a similar order on August 19.

The authorities in other districts of Uttar Pradesh, including Azamgarh, Ballia, Basti, Balrampur, Shamli and Agra, followed suit, Live Law quoted the petition as stating.

The petitioner argued that the restrictions violate the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution. The three articles protect the rights to equality, freedom and life and personal liberty.

Jain was arrested on August 18, along with former Delhi Jal Board Chief Executive Officer Udit Prakash Rai and four others, by the Anti-Corruption Branch. It is unclear if the other accused persons have also been granted bail.
